text: People ask which recipe to start with. The honest answer is that the pot decides more than the recipe does.
Heavy, with a lid that actually seals

A braise wants an even, gentle heat and its own steam kept inside. Cast iron with an enamelled interior does both: the mass evens out the oven cycling, and the weight of the lid keeps the humidity in. A thin pan with a loose lid gives you scorched patches and a dry surface in the same dish.
Narrow enough that the liquid comes up

The single most common failure is a pot too wide for the amount of food. Liquid should reach roughly two thirds up the meat. In a pot that is too wide it barely covers the base, evaporates in the first hour, and the braise becomes a roast.
If your only pot is wide, use less meat rather than more liquid. Diluting a braise to fill a pot is how you get pale, watery stew.
Brand, colour, and whether the handles are brass. A £40 pot with a heavy base and a tight lid outperforms a beautiful thin one every time.

text: Every recipe here fits the same shape: brown something, soften aromatics, add liquid, then leave it alone for a long time. Learn the shape and the recipes become variations rather than instructions.

The scaling works. Drag the servings control on any recipe and the quantities move with it, including the awkward ones — a third of an onion is still a third of an onion, and the site says so rather than rounding it away.
Times are measured, not copied. When a recipe says the shin needs three hours, it is because it needed three hours in a domestic oven at 150°C, in a pot with the lid on.

text: Braising is not “slow roasting with liquid”. It is a specific transformation, and knowing which one tells you when a dish is done.
The change you are waiting for

Tough cuts are tough because of collagen. Below about 70°C collagen just sits there. Above it, given enough time in the presence of water, it converts to gelatine — which is why a shin that was rubbery at two hours is silky at three, and why the sauce thickens without any flour.

That conversion is slow and temperature-sensitive. Hotter is not faster in any useful sense: at 200°C the outside of the meat dries and tightens long before the middle has had its three hours, and you end up with strings in a thin sauce.

Keep the oven at 150°C and the liquid at a bare tremble, never a boil. Keep the lid on: the point is a humid environment, not reduction. Reduce at the end, with the lid off and the meat lifted out, when you can taste what you are reducing.
And stop testing with a timer. The dish is ready when a spoon goes through the meat with no resistance — three hours is a prediction, not a rule.

text: This is the recipe I make when I want the week to be easier. It takes twenty minutes of attention at the start, twenty at the end, and three hours in between where the oven does the work.
The only step worth being fussy about is the browning. Pale beef makes a pale ragù, and no amount of simmering recovers it.
1.2 kg beef shin, on the bone, cut into thick slices
800 g canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
Dry the beef properly and salt it. Brown it hard in oil, in batches, until the surface is genuinely dark — this is the only chance the dish gets to build that flavour. Lift it out and keep it.

Drop the heat. Cook the onion, carrot and celery in the same fat with a pinch of salt until soft and sweet, about fifteen minutes. Add the garlic for a minute, then the tomato purée, and cook until it darkens.
Pour in the wine, scrape everything off the base, and let it reduce until the smell of alcohol is gone.

Return the beef, add the tomatoes and bay, and top up with water until the liquid comes two thirds up the meat. Bring to a bare simmer, lid on, and put it in a 150°C oven. Leave it alone for three hours.

Lift out the beef, discard the bones, and shred the meat with two forks. Reduce the sauce uncovered until it clings to a spoon, then return the meat and season properly. It will taste better tomorrow.
Cook the pappardelle a minute short, finish it in the sauce with a splash of pasta water, and serve with parmesan and parsley.
The sauce freezes better than almost anything else in this book. Freeze it without the pasta, in portions.
No shin? Oxtail works and is better; chuck works and is fine. Avoid anything lean.
Doubling this is free — the oven does not care. The browning is the only step that takes longer.

text: The first time I made this I salted it like a normal braise and it was inedible. Preserved lemons and olives are both salt-delivery systems; the stock and the seasoning have to make room for them.
2 preserved lemons, flesh discarded, skin sliced thin
Salt the thighs and lay them skin-down in a dry, wide pan over medium heat. Do not move them. Let the fat render and the skin go deep gold — eight to ten minutes. Turn once, then lift them out.
Pour off most of the fat. Cook the onions in what is left until soft and golden, then add garlic, cumin, ginger and saffron for a minute.
Return the thighs skin-up, add the stock so it comes halfway up but leaves the skin proud, and simmer covered at a low heat until the meat pulls from the bone.
Add the preserved lemon and olives, cook uncovered for ten minutes to reduce, and finish with coriander. Taste before salting — the lemons and olives bring plenty.
Keeping the skin above the liquid is the whole trick; submerged skin goes flabby and there is no fixing it.
Preserved lemon is worth buying rather than substituting. Fresh lemon is a different, sharper thing.

text: This starter recipe exists so the cookbook has something to render on day one. Replace it, or copy its front matter for your own recipes — yield, times, ingredients groups and steps drive the scaler, the unit switch and the timings bar.
400 g canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
Bring a large pot of water to the boil, salt it well, and cook the spaghetti one minute short of the packet time.
Warm the oil in a wide skillet, soften the garlic without colouring it, add the tomatoes and simmer until glossy.
Drag the pasta into the sauce with a splash of its water, toss over high heat for a minute, and finish with basil.
Swap the basil for parsley in winter; add chilli flakes with the garlic for heat.

text: Fennel behaves like two different vegetables depending on how long you cook it. Twenty minutes gives you something aniseedy and assertive. An hour gives you something sweet and almost jammy, which is what this dish wants.
Soaked overnight. Two 400g tins work; skip to step three.
2 fennel bulbs, quartered, core left in
½ cup flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
For pouring over at the table.
Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water, bring to a hard boil for ten minutes, then simmer until almost tender — 40 to 60 minutes depending on their age. Keep the cooking water.
Meanwhile, brown the fennel quarters in oil on their cut sides until they take real colour. Add the onion and cook until soft, then the garlic, fennel seeds and chilli for a minute more.
Add the beans with enough of their water plus the stock to just cover. Season, bring to a tremble, cover, and cook at 160°C until the beans are creamy and the fennel yields to a spoon.
Off the heat, stir through lemon zest and juice and most of the parsley. Let it sit for ten minutes — it thickens as it cools. Pour over the good oil at the table.
Salt the beans only once they are tender if they are old; young beans can be salted from the start.
Leftovers become soup with a splash of stock, or a bruschetta topping crushed onto toast.
